# Falsifiability (risky, testable predictions) (`falsifiability`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/ideas.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Scientific method & philosophical ideas (`ideas`)
- Deps: helped by scientific_method, formal_logic
- Core idea: A claim about the world is only informative if it forbids something, so that some possible observation would show it to be wrong. A thousand agreeing cases cannot prove 'all swans are white', one black swan refutes it; so look for the test most likely to fail, and say beforehand what result would make you give the idea up. An explanation that fits every outcome (the patient recovered because of the remedy, or died because it was given too late) explains nothing. The convincing move is a risky prediction made in public, like Halley's in 1705 that the comet of 1682 would return about the end of 1758.
- Pitfalls:
  - Confusing 'falsifiable' with 'false' or 'falsified'; a good theory is falsifiable and has survived the attempts
  - Claiming one failed prediction kills a theory: the test also depends on instruments and side assumptions (Uranus's deviation led to Neptune, not to the end of Newton)
  - Presenting Popper's criterion as the agreed definition of science; philosophers and working scientists treat it as one useful test among others
  - Calling unfalsifiable statements meaningless or worthless; ethics, mathematics and religion are simply not empirical claims
  - Demanding that a diviner or priest name in advance what would prove him wrong is a public challenge to his office
- History: greece: c. 450 BC onwards – refutation by counterexample and reductio (Zeno, Socrates); applies to arguments, not yet to experiments; china: c. 80 AD – Wang Chong refutes omen and ghost beliefs by drawing consequences that do not occur; islamic: c. 1021 – Ibn al-Haytham designs experiments to decide between rival theories of vision; europe: 1620 – Bacon: 'the force of the negative instance is greater' (Novum Organum I.46); 1758 return of Halley's comet; 1919 eclipse test of general relativity; 1934 Popper, Logik der Forschung (English 1959)
- Read:
  - Karl Popper, The Logic of Scientific Discovery (1959)
  - Karl Popper, Conjectures and Refutations (1963)
  - Peter Godfrey-Smith, Theory and Reality: An Introduction to the Philosophy of Science (2003)
